utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please. I see Mr. Gajic on his feet. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, certain exhibits marked for identification because there were no translation, whether into the Serbian or into the Croatian language, have now been entered into e-court. So by your leave I will read out the exhibit numbers. These are D156, D175, D188, D189, D191, D194, D205, D207, D208, D223, D238, D240, D242, D245, D246, D247, D250, D251, D270, D282, D283, D284, and finally D285. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, these exhibits are no longer MFI'd, but in evidence. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. If we could go back to P22, maybe it will save a little bit time if we can get it up on the screen while Mr. Butler comes in. It's where we left off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made yesterday at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see you've got your same binder. If you could go to where we left off, it should be tab 4, the six strategic objectives. We also see them up on the screen. And really for our purposes I just want to ask you, looking at number 3: "Establish a corridor in the Drina River valley, that is, eliminate the Drina as a border separating Serbian States." Can you tell us the Drina river valley as you understand it in this document, does that include the area from Srebrenica to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That area is generally referred to as the lower Drina valley or lower Podrinje. So that particular geographic area would be encompassed on the west bank of the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you talked a little bit yet about the Assembly session in May where these were talked about. Let's go to tab 5, if we could. Were you able to review any minutes of that Assembly meeting? And it should be 65 ter 25.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 13 in the English and B/C/S page 12. There we see the front page indicating minutes very briefly. Now if we can go to 13 in the English and 12 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, could you take a look in the English, it's the middle of the paragraph -- it's the middle of the page, it's the second paragraph, sort of the last line, it says: "The first such goal is separation from the other two ethnic communities - separation of states." Now, if we go back - and I don't think we need to take the time to do it - but if we go back to page 7 in English we can see that the person that's speaking is Karadzic. Does that fit your recollection of the person that's speaking at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And that is the first goal that we saw on the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see, as we go down, it's page 13 in the B/C/S, paragraph 3 in the B/C/S, but it's still page 13 of the English, where it talks about that -- that third strategic goal that we talked -- that mentioned the Drina river valley and again mentions the elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds. And we can -- I won't read it all. We can -- we can see it ourselves. It talks about the possibility of some Muslim municipalities to be set up along the Drina as enclaves in order for them to achieve their rights. And it says: "But that belt along the Drina must basically belong to the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." And it talks about strategically useful. Was this a strategic area in your view in some way for the Serbian politic at this -- the politicians at this early stage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly, what was your understanding of its importance to them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one looks at a map of the Republika Srpska, the key geographic feature is that area along the Drina River which is somewhat narrow but connects the two main bodies of where the ethnic Bosnian Serbs were residing in the Krajina and further down south in Herzegovina. The Drina river valley region in 1992 when the conflict started was primarily populated by Bosnians of Muslim ethnicity. Serbs were the minority in those regions. It was recognised that there could be no chance of success of their political goals. Early on it was to be joined with the remainder of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, and then later their own autonomous state if the situation persisted, that they remained the minority population in the Drina valley. So they understood from a geo-political sense that they had to become the dominant force in population in that area in order to secure that territory for the future of the state of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think I'll leave that subject alone for now, but that -- I just -- that is important to get established early on. Now, in your review in your studies and your report, you did mention that you reviewed the laws applicable in the region at the time and the military rules. In your view, did -- were you able to determine whether or not the SFRY, the former Yugoslavia, before the war had a system of laws that reflected the laws of armed conflict as promulgated in the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As a component of the criminal code of the former SFRY, one particular section of that code dealt with crimes that were consistent with the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were those laws -- were you able to determine whether those SFRY laws were ever adopted into the RS legal system upon its formation or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in 1993 the Bosnian Serb leadership formally took the step of redesignating the criminal code of the SFRY to be the criminal code of the Republika Srpska, with just minor variations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the JNA officers, the professional military officers like General Tolimir that were part of the JNA before the war, did they receive any training from their military -- well, rules or programmes in the laws of armed conflict, the Geneva -- the laws of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces of the former SFRY did publish regulations on how to apply the laws of armed conflict, and they were of course distributed throughout the military. And based on my research and interviews with various former military officers, not only from the Republika Srpska but from other republics that later became independent from Yugoslavia, as a component of the professional development and training of officers at various levels, refresher training was required in these particular conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, moving on to it becoming the VRS and people -- General Mladic, General Tolimir, General Milovanovic, and the others, did the VRS in any way adopt any regulations themselves that would reflect the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, very early on in the conflict, President Karadzic, as the president of the then-Bosnian Serb Presidency, passed a decree which directed that the regulations on the application of the law of war to the SFRY apply to the armed conflict and the forces of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I know you deal with this in your reports, but I would like to go over some of the materials that you have cited regarding this topic. And just briefly, briefly discuss, if we could -- go to tab 6, 65 -- and I'm sorry, thank you -- we need to tender 65 ter 25, the Assembly minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 25 shall be assigned Exhibit P2477. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now if we could go to 65 ter 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's the next tab, should be tab 6. And we see here this document entitled: "The Main Staff of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska, Military Prosecutor's Office at the Main Staff of the Armed Forces." And it's entitled: "Guide-lines for Determining the Criteria for Criminal Prosecution." And it's dated down at the bottom -- well, we can't see it on the screen, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could bring the screen up a little bit maybe we will be able to see the year there. Yes, it should be in both, in the original -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you very briefly tell us what this document is, very briefly, and then we'll go over just a few pieces of it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Early in the conflict, I believe this document is dated to roughly October of 1992, the Main Staff, particularly the military prosecutor's office - which at that time worked and served the Main Staff before it was transferred to the Ministry of Defence - laid out a number of provisions for prosecuting crimes against the armed forces. This not only included acts related to avoiding military service or acts directed against the army, but also directed against crimes that were committed in violation of international law during an armed conflict. This document lays out in general terms those different types of activities and what provisions of law apply as well as in general terms how both the military prosecutors as well as senior officers of the army would be expected to counter these types of criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page in both languages. Sorry, we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S. I'm sorry, the next -- we're fine in the English and, I'm sorry, I don't have the exact B/C/S page. I've just decided to go -- to do this is why. Let's stay with page 2 in the English and I want -- let's go to the next page in the B/C/S -- actually, no, stay right there. It's number 1 that I want to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's look at the bottom of page 2 in the English, it's also the bottom of the page that we have in the B/C/S, where, I think you'll agree, it lists three main criminal offence categories that it's concerned with prosecuting, and that is the failure to respond to the military call-up is number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then if we could flip the page in the B/C/S. Could we go to the next page in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then number 2 is wilfully absenting oneself from one's post. So I think we can all understand that failure to call-up and leaving your post are two pretty critical parts of running an army in a war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So let's go to number 3 which is on the next page in English. And here we see number 3, the last number that they have is the criminal offences against humanity and international law pursuant to the chapter of the criminal code. Is this what you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 7 in the English, should be page 25 in the B/C/S. And this is the chapter in this document under number 3 that we just saw reflecting the criminal offences against humanity and international law. Yes, that's -- that's where it begins in the B/C/S, but I think if we could just take a look at that in the B/C/S and then go to the next page in the B/C/S is where I just want to ask you a few things of what you think of these. And of course it starts out that the -- as we see, that the legal classification of these criminal offences were adopted from the international conventions. And from your review of this document, would you agree with that first statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on in that first paragraph to say: "The unique nature of these criminal offences is also in their seriousness, which is expressed in severe punishments, including the death penalty for six criminal offences." So did they actually have the death penalty for these offences?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time under their law, they in fact had a death penalty for these offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now going to the next paragraph, and this is where I have B/C/S page 25, paragraph 2, it says: "Crimes against humanity and international law can be committed by individuals acting on their own, but by their nature these criminal offences are usually committed in an organised fashion in the implementation of the policy of the ruling circles. Most of these criminal offences are committed only during armed conflicts or are in some way closely connected with armed conflicts, which means that they are committed within the context of broad military operations and on the orders from superior officers." And I don't want to get into this in any sort of detail, Mr. Butler, but when you read this and know what you know about the charges related to Srebrenica, does this paragraph reflect in any way the -- the allegations as you know them to be in -- regarding the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe it's a very accurate statement of the circumstances that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8 in the English. It should be B/C/S page 27, the last paragraph of page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's that top paragraph, and we'll see from the -- just the previous page it talks about the army is obligated to observe international laws. And then it says: "From this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the Army of Republika Srpska as the giver of orders in command of the armed forces, whose members could commit or are committing some of these offences, to take uncompromising action and prevent such conduct. This responsibility belongs by its nature particularly to high-ranking individuals and officials in state, military, or public organisations who are in the concrete circumstances in a position to issue orders." Now, looking at this -- and I want to see if you think this can apply to General Tolimir, because I note that it's speaking of the officer corps of the army as the giver of orders in command of the armed forces. Was General Tolimir in your view at the time of the events in Srebrenica a commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a commander of a formation per se, but in the context of this particular paragraph he would certainly qualify as a senior or commanding officer, one of those high -- the highest-ranking officers on the Main Staff, those individuals who are the ultimate giver of orders, to use the phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he have any subordinates under him who he, under the rules, could issue orders directly to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were those top people, as you recall them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would include his two principal deputies, Colonel Beara, Colonel Salapura, and the other members of the intelligence and security staff, Colonel Jankovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Pesarevic"], all of those officers that worked in that particular -- those particular branches, the intelligence, the security, and the military police, those people fell directly under the control of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the second name you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Beara, Colonel Salapura and other members of the security staff, that would include Colonel Jankovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic and all of those other officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was only asking you for the last name --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you just mentioned because that is not recorded correctly. Please repeat that name after Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Keserovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Kesarovic"], K-e-s-e-r-o-v-i-c. Close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please look at the screen if it is spelled correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't look like it's spelled correctly, but I think it's close enough. I think -- we have several documents in here which will actually list his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I do think that's important, as Your Honour knows, so we best -- for the record, if we could get the -- I think we'll all agree the correct spelling is K-e-s-e-r-o-v-i-c, and I think we'll all remember him as testifying here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I indeed have asked the witness to give us the right spelling. Would you agree that this is the man you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to the -- it's the bottom of page 8 in the English, it should be page 31 on the B/C/S. And it's just that last -- second to the last sentence: "So that the command of the Main Staff has a full understanding of the types and number of these criminal offences, all unit commands shall ..." And then it says: " ... work on uncovering all war crimes against humanity and international law on the territory in their area of responsibility. "Inform the closest military police, security, and military judicial organs about any crime they discover ..." And then we can see the rest. I won't go over all of them. In your review of all the materials in the Srebrenica case, did you find any indication that the VRS or RS authorities during the war time ever investigated or prosecuted or punished any VRS soldier for crimes against Muslims, civilians, POWs, related to the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly explain the sorts of materials that you've had a chance to review that would have indicated the presence of any such investigations or prosecutions or punishments, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a component of the investigation at a certain point in time, I believe approximately 1998 or 1999, we were able to obtain documents from the various military prosecutor's offices of the Army of the Republika Srpska or at that time is of Ministry of Defence, which laid out their monthly reports and detailed their investigative activities, the crimes that were under investigation. And we were able to, of course, do the same thing through interviewing various officials of the military prosecutor's office and the military court system. The general theme that came out of that was when one looked at all of these documents and interviews, there was very little attempt, despite the widespread knowledge of the crimes that occurred, for anyone to take on an investigation or prosecution. In fact, I'm only aware of two pro forma, if you will, investigations that took place related to Srebrenica that were instituted by the government -- the Republika Srpska government and military in 1995 and 1996, one of which the RS MUP concluded that the victims had all killed themselves or were battle casualties. And another one specifically related to the discovery of mass graves in Branjevo. The person put in charge of investigating that incident was Colonel Beara, which led to a predictable result of that investigation going nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to get back again briefly to our -- the area of law. We saw a bit of what the prosecutor -- Office of the Prosecutor had to say early on in the war. Could we go to the next tab, it should be 7, it's 65 ter -- oh, and I'm sorry, I keep forgetting to -- I want to of course tender that last exhibit, it's 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 28 shall be accompanied Exhibit P2478. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we go to 65 ter 401. And I will -- we can see that this is entitled: "Law on the Amendments to the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia." What is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document is an excerpt of the Republika Srpska Official Gazette, which is the document by which the government publicly announced its orders, decrees, regulations, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 401 shall be assigned Exhibit P2479. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could now go to 65 ter 679.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for it, we can see that this is chapter -- called chapter 16 of the criminal offences against humanity and international law." Do you recall, is this related to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, if you were to look at Exhibit P2479, Article 1, it specifically notes that the Criminal Code of the former SFRJ is essentially renamed the Criminal Code of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as we can see - and I won't spend a lot of time on it - we can see on this first page it's the genocide and that definition of genocide is similar to that -- is it similar to that that you're used to in this court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have the respective page in B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I -- if we could go to the next page. I'm sorry. That's obviously not it. Perhaps it's the next page. Well, let's go to page 66 in the B/C/S. Sorry for that small glitch there. We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is that definition of genocide similar to what you're used to dealing with in this court and other courts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see the next war crimes against the civilian population, which, as we look at it, includes attack on a civilian population. In the middle of the paragraph it says unlawful deportation, transfers, exposing the population to starvation. And here we also see the punishments for genocide is not less than five years in prison or by the death penalty. And as we go through these pages, we will see the other counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could be -- go to page -- the other laws. Let's go to page 68 in the B/C/S. It should be the third page in the English. And this is a specific law against war crimes against prisoners of war which is set out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't think we need to go through this further except to perhaps acknowledge, are there a whole panoply of international war crimes in this section?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence, 679.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 679 shall be assigned Exhibit P2480. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So those were the laws that became part of the Republika Srpska. Now let's go to 65 ter 399. That should be tab 9. We have another section of the gazette. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This particular section of the Official Gazette lays out the order by President Karadzic on the application of the rules of international law of war on the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we flip the next page in the B/C/S. We see it's -- this is number 198 and we've got to go over to finish up the 198 to see the president's name on the bottom and the full text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter document 399 shall be assigned Exhibit P2481. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now could we go to the next tab, and it's 65 ter 680. And as we're waiting I can note that this is entitled "regulations on the application of international laws of war and the armed forces of the SFRY."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we need to flip - I'm sorry - the next page in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this -- is this related at all to the law we just saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Based on those laws, laws of course being broadly written, the military of the SFRY, the armed forces, subsequently took it upon themselves to more clearly define in terms of rules and regulations how those laws would be applied and followed within the military. This particular document reflects in a substantial amount of detail how that is to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 62 in English. It should be B/C/S page 56. So did these rules apply to the VRS during the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be paragraph 207 that I would like in the B/C/S. Thank you. And of course this is the same in English. It's at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's entitled: "Basic rights of prisoners of war." And it's entitled: "Responsibility of the State for Treatment of Prisoners of War by its Nationals." And it says: "Prisoners of war are under the authority of the Detaining Power, and not," we need to go to the next page in English, "and not of the individual persons or military units which capture them. The Detaining Power shall be responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war. This responsibility does not rule out the personal responsibility of individuals." Now, Mr. Butler, we have moved into the area, as you've stated, of military regulations. Can you tell us, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially what this paragraph reflects is that individual prisoners of war who are captured by either members of the other armed forces or by other means become the responsibility of the state as a whole to safe-guard. The highest levels of the government, be they military or civilian, cannot escape responsibility for overseeing the proper treatment of prisoners of war by arguing that the responsibility to safe-guard and properly detain those individuals rested with lower-level individuals or with discrete military units. So it is a collective responsibility that ultimately is placed at the highest level of political and military power of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, would the Main Staff of the VRS and its members be included as an authority of the detaining power?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff, being the highest body within the Army of the Republika Srpska, would certainly qualify as an authority of the detaining power in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's look briefly at 209: "Prohibition of reprisals. "Reprisals against prisoners of war are prohibited in all cases." In the context of armed conflict, what is your definition of what a reprisal is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of a reprisal is a deliberate decision by a warring party to deliberately commit a war crime for the select purpose of seeking to prevent the continued commission of war crimes by the other party. It is, in essence, reciprocal treatment. It is used only in very limited cases when there is no other apparent alternative to prevent the opposing warring party from engaging in their own commission of war crimes. The feature about it is, one, given that it is a deliberate commission of a criminal act, those decisions are normally taken only at the very highest levels of the military or the government to undertake such a reprisal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the specific situation that we're talking about here, reprisals against prisoners of war, in this rule it says that it's prohibited in all cases. Is your understanding -- are there any exceptions in the rules of the former Yugoslavia that would allow for reprisals against prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we can go to just briefly again I -- to paragraphs 213, that should be 63 in the English, 57 in the B/C/S. Paragraph 213 talks about the beginning of captivity and that it's prohibited to wound or kill a member of the enemy armed forces, of course. And if we can go on to page 64 in the English, page 57 in the B/C/S, it talks about the personal belongs of prisoners of war. I won't read that, but it talks about protecting the personal belongings. 217 talks about evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would these rules have been well known in your view to the senior officers, the professional officers of the VRS, such as General Tolimir, General Mladic, General Krstic, Colonel Blagojevic, Colonel Pandurevic, Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic, and others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And there's another document on a very related topic I wanted to ask you about, though I should offer this -- these regulations into evidence. They are 680.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 680 shall be assigned Exhibit P2482. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to 65 ter 2226. I believe as we're waiting for that to come up and it should be 11 in the tabs, you were able to -- were you able to identify an actual war time document that spoke of one of these rules that we had just gone over? And I'll hope to get this up. That's not it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is correct. The English version is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps -- are you sure that's P --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now the English version is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that my numbers or -- just for my information? It wasn't. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is from the command of the Drina Corps dated 15 July 1993, a time-period we don't usually deal with too often, but -- and it's -- if we go to the -- just look at the next page in English. I don't think we need to do that on the screen, but we can see that it's from a person named deputy commander Colonel Milutin Skocajic, pardon the pronunciation, and it's to all the commands, all the brigades. I take it that's all the commands and brigades, units, in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's entitled: "Treatment of prisoners of war." And it's -- begins by talking about the Muslim sabotage groups. But what I want to ask you about is in the middle of that first paragraph and this statement: "From the moment they are captured, enemy soldiers who are put out of action must be treated as prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Convention. Actions contrary to international and domestic law constitute serious criminal offences. In addition to criminal responsibility, persons acting in this way also incur all other types of responsibility." This is the part I wanted to ask you about. "This responsibility rests not only with the immediate perpetrators of criminal offences and inhumane treatment, but also by their superior officers, because prisoners of war are not the property of individuals or military units, but the responsibility of the VRS and the RS." In your view, does this relate to one of the rules you just went over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I think we'll recall from the rule we went over it mentioned those in command that had the power to issue orders. This does not say that. It says "... but also their superior officers ..." What do you make of that difference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it reflects simply an issue of semantics in language. The phrase in the regulations and the applications define a superior officer with respect to responsibility and does not limit responsibility only to those individuals designated as a "commander." It also designates it as any superior officer being any officer who has an ability to prevent the commission of crimes or to punish individuals afterwards. So a derivative responsibility for failing to ensure prisoners of war in this particular case are not properly cared for and that crimes are not committed against them. That liability is not strictly limited to commanders. It's limited to all officers who are in a position to have prevented such acts and failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, clearly this is a corps document going to its brigades, but taking this principle higher as we saw in that rule, in your view would General Tolimir have had the power to issue orders to stop any conduct -- prevent or stop any conduct by Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same question for General -- as we know him now General Keserovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Radoslav Jankovic, Colonel Salapura?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer -- excuse me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just take note of this last -- this will be the last sentence in the bottom paragraph in the English. It's the second paragraph in the B/C/S. It says: "All violations of the provisions of the international laws of war and humanitarian laws should be immediately reported and punitive measures taken. In this activity, it is extremely significant to point out the political, moral, and humanitarian importance of our treatment of prisoners of war, because we are fully justified in demanding that the enemy side treat our prisoners of war in the same way." What is Skocajic basically saying here to his people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, he's noting the obvious fact that it's difficult to demand the other party or parties to a conflict comply with the provisions of humane treatment of prisoners of war when, as the other side of the coin, your party is not doing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I -- oh, and Milutin Skocajic is not a name we've heard much about. Do you know what happened to him after 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this period he is the Chief of Staff/deputy commander of the Drina Corps. I believe at some point in 1995 he becomes a general and is appointed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I'd offer that into evidence, 2226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 2226 shall be assigned Exhibit P2483. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That -- well, I know you've dealt with that more in depth in your report. I think the basic rules, the Geneva Conventions and the rules, as are set out by the VRS, I think I will leave that section now and get into some more particular areas of concerns and the rules associated more with intelligence and security and command, which has of course been an issue in this case. And to start off that I would like to go to P1112.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, a document you're -- you've seen several times, so I won't ask Mr. Butler to go into it in a lot of detail. But I would like to ask him to help clarify some issues which I think are important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we see this document is a 24 October 1994 document from the Main Staff and if we -- we see at the end of it, it was signed for the commander. Could we go to the last page in the B/C/S. We don't need the English as yet. And I believe that has been -- I think the general will agree with me, that has been identified -- that signature is that of General Tolimir. So getting back to the first page, now did you spend a fair amount of time in your reports and in your testimony outlining and analysing the regulations that define the roles and responsibilities of the security officer in relation to the -- working within a command, at a brigade, at a corps level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we've seen a lot of those in this case, so I'm going to save some time by not going over them. But in that respect we can see - and I'm sure the General will agree with me - that these rules outline those basic rules. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge of the rules associated with the security and intel branch, do you find anything different about these instructions, that is, shortened view of the rules themselves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. These are consistent with the broader regulations and rules on the application of intelligence and security within the former SFRY, which were adopted and utilised by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to ask you to give us a hand with some of these concepts. Under "instructions," number 1 it says: "The field work of the VRS security and intelligence organs primarily includes intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks which, depending on the situation, make-up about 80 per cent of their total engagement. The remaining 20 per cent of their engagement consists of administrative and staff, military police and criminal-legal tasks and duties."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, one correction. Line 2 of page 25 in your quotation the first words read as follows, "the field work of the VRS." I see in the text "the field of work of the VRS." I think this is a significant difference. It's not "the field work" but "the field of work."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think you're absolutely right, and when I said it, it didn't sound right, and I'm glad you caught it because -- yes, it's much broader than field work and I'm -- thank you for catching that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we have had VRS officers talk to us about each of these concepts. I think you have recently, as you described your job, described what intelligence, military intelligence, work is. So I won't ask you to repeat that. But as intelligence work is mentioned in this document, is that similar or -- to the work you described? When you described what intelligence work was, I think it was in response to Judge Mindua's question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we won't go over that again. Can you tell us in the context of this document and the VRS work, what is counter-intelligence and what -- and we'll get to some examples. But can you -- counter-intelligence is -- I sometimes find that a difficult concept. But can you tell us fundamentally what your view of what counter-intelligence is? What does it amount to be in the army? And of course what I'm talking about is your understanding of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In probably the most basic of language, it is the steps that in this particular context that the VRS undertook in order to prevent the opposing forces, in their case the armed forces of the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats, from learning about the plans, policies, and essential elements of information that the VRS sought to maintain for themselves. It, very simply, is defined as the steps that you take in order to prevent your adversaries from gaining intelligence information about your friendly forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- would it be fair to define that as protecting against threats from the outside from the forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term of art can run the range of activities from simple security to prevent the inadvertent disclosure of confidential military documents because they are left unattended, all the way to the most sophisticated operations designed to uncover and neutralise opposing espionage networks directed against your forces. It covers a very wide range of activities that are important for militaries to undertake in order to safe-guard critical information about itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in each of those answers you've spoken of -- I believe of the enemy finding out important information. Can counter-intelligence work involve looking into your own forces for threats from within, such as traitors or that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the identification and elimination of subversive elements within your own armed forces would certainly fall as a counter-intelligence-related task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If counter-intelligence work, as you've said, it would be to protect the secrets of an army, what was -- and just briefly, what was General Tolimir's role in -- first of all, at what level was he in the counter-intelligence hierarchy of officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Tolimir was the pinnacle of that effort by the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would General Milovanovic and General Mladic rely on him for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, would a -- the plans associated with a military operation, keeping those plans and details of that military operation, would that be part of General Tolimir's job, to keep out of the hands of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about an operation as charged in this indictment, to murder able-bodied -- thousands of able-bodied men, an operation to detain them, transport them to execution sites, summarily execute them, and bury them, and re-bury them, would that be a kind of a military secret?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In context, if you are seeking to prevent any public disclosure of your involvement in those acts, your security and counter-intelligence organs would play a very large part in making sure that disclosure did not occur. So again, as the head of the -- you know, as the -- more accurately, as the assistant commander for intelligence and security for the Main Staff of the army, General Tolimir -- that effort revolves around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think we can all agree that finding out the date of an attack and the location of an attack is a critical detail that cannot fall in the hands of the enemy. But would it be a military problem for the VRS if the enemy or the international community found out that the VRS had engaged in an organised effort to summarily execute thousands of able-bodied Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As foreshadowed in 1992 and 1993 in some of the previous documents discussed, the army leadership recognised that it would have dramatic negative consequences to the political and military conduct of the war if -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue. After that, Mr. Tolimir will get the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. If they were involved in such activities -- and in 1995, in July of 1995, when one looks at the activities and one then looks at the consequences that occurred afterwards, they're factually correct. The public disclosure of the involvement of the Army of the Republika Srpska in these crimes had a significantly negative impact on them militarily as well as the political leverage the Republika Srpska had to end the war on terms favourable to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish peace onto this house, that this day of judgement should end in keeping with God's will, not mine. And please, I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor would not ask leading questions in order to elicit an answer that is in the sphere of speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said speculative questions, speculative questions. It was interpreted as "leading" and it's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think fundamentally my question was: Would a murder operation -- what effect, if any, would the public disclosure of a murder operation have militarily on the VRS? I don't think that's speculation. There's been a murder operation charged in this case. I think we -- that is certainly not speculation at this point in the Tribunal, that large numbers of people were murdered. So I think it's a fair question and I don't think it's speculative. What effect would that have? My point is: A very large secret, be it the landing date or a secret like this, could it be harmed if it gets out? Not speculative in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think in this trial we have heard many such questions by both parties. For instance, would it be illogical or would it be logical to draw a conclusion like this and that and that. This happens very often, and if a witness is capable to answer a question of this kind, there is no concern about this kind of questions. It's not misleading. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, were you thinking of anything in particular when you said -- when the -- did the -- well, let me ask you: Did the international community, in your view, become aware of these crimes in any particular way that you think might have had a negative effect on the VRS or RS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the public disclosure of these crimes, particularly as the scale, the numbers of missing, grew, did have a political effect on the willingness of NATO to overtly engage in activities against the Republika Srpska in the subsequent months, August, September, October, leading up to the end of the war. In part because of those activities by NATO, coupled with the Croatian military invasion Operation Storm, when the war terminated effectively with the Dayton Peace Agreements, the Republika Srpska was somewhat smaller geographically than it had been in July of 1995. So in that context the Srebrenica crimes had an extremely adverse military and political impact in the future, in subsequent months, August, September, October, on the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular public announcement in August that created this international awareness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm not sure of the exact date, but in August of 1995 then-secretary of -- I believe she was at the time either Secretary of State or the Ambassador -- the US Ambassador of the United Nations, Albright, disclosed US reconnaissance photographs, laying out photographic evidence of mass executions that had occurred related to Srebrenica before the UN Security Council. And in going public with this information, it significantly had a -- it had a significantly adverse effect against political and the military interest of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just one last question. So had that operation to murder people been kept secret, would that have been better for the VRS and RS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is: Yes, it would. And when one examines the activities of the Army of the Republika Srpska following the public disclosure of those crimes where they engaged in an effort to essentially exhume the primary mass graves and conceal the victims in more remote secondary and tertiary sites, I would say that that opinion was also shared by the leadership of the Republika Srpska and their military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. McCloskey. We must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before you continue your examination-in-chief, I would like to remind you that we are expecting some explanations in relation to six witnesses by the end of today's hearing, especially Michael Hedley, Johan de Koeijer, and four female witnesses from Srebrenica. You promised that we get -- receive an update by the end of this week, and hopefully we can get some more information that will assist us in planning of the remainder of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President. I am expecting that. I've been working on Mr. de Koeijer myself with Mr. Gajic and we'll try to resolve something on that, and I'm expecting clear information on the other five very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "very soon"? Can we expect to receive some update by the end of today's hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, no question about it, and your enunciation of this is certainly helpful in that regard. So I will get it and we will get it to you this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Still concentrating on this document P1112, the instructions from 24 October that have left the screen for a bit, and especially that paragraph number 1 that we've been talking about that mentioned intelligence and counter-intelligence being 80 per cent of the work of the security person. Does -- in your judgement, do security officers at the brigade, corps, Main Staff level have any responsibilities related to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is the topic mentioned -- is there any mention -- we don't see any mentions of prisoners of war in this document or in this paragraph. Is the general topic mentioned anywhere that would include this sort of work in any of these paragraphs? I'm looking at -- starting off with paragraph 1, of course.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. In the particular document and in the context of the tasks involved, due to their supervisory functions of the military police organs of the army and the role of military police in the handling and securing of prisoners of war, by extension security officers are part of that process. It would be their responsibilities to advise the commander of -- and may essentially make proposals on the best way for military police or others to handle these prisoners, the processes and procedures to be used, particularly as they relate to the military police. And then of course the commander would make these decisions as to whether or not to follow these proposals or to modify them in some manner. So in that respect, due to the role of the military police in the dealings of prisoners of war and securing them, the security officers do have a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, once a commander, be it a brigade, a corps, or the Main Staff, makes a decision related to the military police and the securing or dealing with prisoners, does the security officer have any responsibility at that point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As a subordinate to the commander, the security officer actively works to implement the commander's orders in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want you to get into any of the facts and detail of this case, but has your review and investigation revealed security officers at the brigade, corps, and Main Staff level dealing with prisoners and military police issues from July 12th through the 16th and -- well, and beyond?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There is extensive counter -- or basically activities related to security officers, military police, and prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- so does this paragraph -- it makes a reference to this 20 per cent. Does that 20 per cent of your view that talks about administrative and staff military police, criminal illegal tasks and duties, does that include prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 of this document in the English and it's paragraph 5 in the B/C/S. So it's going to be the next page in the B/C/S. And I just want to call our attention to this under paragraph 5, it says: "Personnel policy and service guidance for members of these organs are the exclusive province of the VRS GS commander and the VRS GS assistant commander for security and intelligence. In this regard, the VRS GS security and intelligence sector takes decisions on transfers, appointments, and assignments to special tasks from their field of work for members of the security and intelligence organs." So I think everyone will agree that at the time of this document and throughout the war, that the assistant commander for security intelligence was General Tolimir. What is it saying he has responsibility here for with -- along with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the realm of the technical tasking - for lack of a better word - the specialised -- the intelligence and security specialised orders that are given, that particular chain, that intelligence and security chain, and the people who are assigned to that at subordinate levels are assigned and are maintained by the security and intelligence sector of the Main Staff. It prevents situations from occurring where in the event of undue tension between a brigade commander and his assistant commander for security, potentially because the commander is under investigation, having the ability to subvert these types of activities by simply removing that officer from his position. So in effect, these provisions are in place to ensure that the ability to perform their specialised tasks related to intelligence and security can be protected from undue influence by the commanders of the various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where does Tolimir fit into this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as the assistant commander for security and intelligence on the Main Staff, he is the pinnacle of this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That is already in evidence, that document. Let's now go to 65 ter 2222, and I just, as we're talking about the responsibility of General Tolimir in the security -- as the assistant commander for security, are you aware of a -- at some point where they, the VRS, decided to change the structure of the intelligence and security sections and some of the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In early 1995 there was a decision made that where they had the ability to do so because they had adequate resources, that it would be advantageous for them to physically split the intelligence and security functions of, for example, a light infantry brigade from one particular group of officers to two groups - the intelligence function being one group, the security function being a separate group of officers - as a matter of being more effective in their functions. This particular document dated 29 January 1995 from the Drina Corps lays out the details of that change.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to page 3 in the English and it's the next page, I believe, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we see that it is in the name of the commander of the Drina Corps at the time, General Zivanovic. And I just wanted to call your attention to -- it looks like the last paragraph under item 7. It says: "The Chief of the GS VRS security and intelligence sector shall regulate the competence, contents, and the manner of preparation of the aforementioned personnel through a special instruction." Again, I think everyone will agree that this is at this time a reference to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's he doing in this, something that may happen as low at the brigade level, why would he be involved in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff recognised correctly, I believe, that intelligence and security functions need to be synchronised throughout the entire scope of the military. Having one particular brigade or one particular corps take certain measures and other units take separate measures without them being fully synchronised is not an effective or an efficient way to do military business. These procedures lay out in part how all of these issues are going to be synchronised by the Main Staff and how they will be translated through the corps commands and through their intelligence and security organs down to the brigades and even lower. It also reflects the fact that there are going to be standardised training standards and other professional bench-marks that these officers are going to be required to meet and maintain, and that as part of this -- those -- the responsibility for doing -- you know, appointing these qualified officers to ensuring that they are appropriately trained and qualified for the position is going to fall under the competence of General Tolimir and his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask one question in this point in time in relation to this sentence and this order. I would like to hear your opinion about this paragraph. It is an order by the commander of the Drina Corps, and he is referring to the assistant commander of the VRS. Is it an order he issued to the assistant commander of the VRS or is it something else? How would you try to understand and explain this paragraph: "The Chief of the General Staff of the VRS security and intelligence sector shall regulate ..." What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As you -- if you refer back to the previous page in English where it discusses the previous Main Staff instructions and paragraph 5, clearly the commander of the Drina Corps is not operating in a vacuum. He has received guidance from the Main Staff. He is essentially articulating that guidance from the Main Staff and making it more directive to his subordinates. He's not ordering in this document the chief of the security administration and the Main Staff to do anything. What he is, in fact, saying is that: I'm directing my subordinates to undertake these activities; and as part of these activities, the chief of the staff -- of the intelligence and security directorate will be responsible for these other issues. He's been told that by the Main Staff, that these powers and authorities are reserved to General Tolimir and his people. He is simply reiterating that fact to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in -- going back to more personnel issues, which I think we've seen in other documents. In your view would General Tolimir have any ability to control who was hired as a security officer at the brigade level, such as -- could he do anything about Momir Nikolic being in the Bratunac Brigade or Drago Nikolic in the Zvornik Brigade and Milorad Trbic in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As stated in these documents, the appointment of those officers, as well as many of the other specialised aspects of their training and mission fall directly under the purview of the assistant commander of the Main Staff for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would this include Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, chief of security of the Drina Corps; and Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Kosoric, chief of intel of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As well as Colonel Beara, Salapura, Radoslav Jankovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic that you've mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The appointments of those individuals would fall directly and squarely into his competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document, 2222, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2222 shall be assigned Exhibit P2484. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, for the next section I would like to go back to prisoners of war and the competence of the security branch in dealing with prisoners of war, and in particular General Tolimir and some of the documents associated with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could start out with 65 ter 3753, it should be 14 in the tabs. And this is a document from the Main Staff intelligence and security sector dated 25 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under chief -- by Chief Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. And if we look at the initials under the original, we see LJB. Do you remember what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe those are the initials for Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember what it means for them to be there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in their convention you have two sets of initials. The initials on the left-hand side are those of the person who actually drafted or authored the document, and then those on the right are the individual who typed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is a Teletype version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so I think we all know and will agree that Teletyped versions that are received by someone else cannot have the signature on it. So can you tell us if Beara -- Colonel Beara drafted this but General Tolimir's name is on it, could this have gone out without General Tolimir reading it and standing behind it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is of course the remote possibility that it might have gone out without him reading it in advance, but given the fact that it is signed in his name, he is responsible for its contents. Generally my experience in this practice is that these types of things don't go out without the concurrence of the man who's ultimately responsible for them. Obviously the possibility exists, but it's highly unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this document itself is, we see, to the Eastern Bosnia Corps command, the commission for exchange of prisoners; the Drina Corps command, commission for exchange of prisoners; Eastern Bosnian Corps and Drina Corps OB department, it is noted here as intelligence department; the central commission for exchange of prisoners; and to D. Buljajic personally for information. Now, as we read this, I -- it is said that: "As opinions (regarding the exchange of the prisoners of war) have been harmonised between the commissions of the 1st KK, the DK, and the IBK commands, we hereby give our approval for the exchange, scheduled for 28 October 1993 ..." In your view, who is this "we" that is being referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This "we" is collectively the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it goes on: "... in which 63 captured Serbian soldiers will be exchanged for 54 Turks, whom we are holding captive." Now, let me ask you about this term, "Turks." We all know that this term is used. We know that the Serbians were referred to as Chetniks. Nobody is on trial here for calling people names, but is there any significance in your military opinion for a document from the Main Staff, from Zdravko Tolimir, referring to the enemy as "Turks"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It generally is not a military acceptable practice to kind of use colourful or derogatory language. You know, military documents by nature tend to be very terse. It's a reflection of just how culturally accepted the use of these pejorative terms were, again, by the rank and file chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of message does that send to the lower command when a person of his rank is referring to the enemy in derogatory terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the more universal tenets of leadership is that subordinates take their cue from the actions and the conduct of their superiors. When the superior commands or organs use that type of language or express those types of views, subordinates understand that that type of behaviour and conduct will, in fact, be tolerated or condoned and that they are free to engage it in themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Getting back to the substance of the document, we can all see that General Tolimir and really Colonel Beara play a role in these -- in the exchange of prisoners decisions. If your view and in your study, would that fit into the normal role of General Tolimir and his sector for intel and security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Not only this but there are a number of documents that reflect the detailed role that the Main Staff, particularly the intelligence and security organ or sector, played in monitoring the process by which prisoners were exchanged between the various warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence, 3753.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 3753 shall be assigned Exhibit P2485. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go on to another document 65 ter 3922. It's the 15 in our books, and it's another document from the Main Staff sector for intelligence and security and dated in 1994 this time, 16 June 1994, to the intelligence department of the Drina Corps entitled "Exchange of Prisoners." And we see it's a multi-page document especially in English, but on the third page - which I don't think we need to go to now because I think we can see it in the Serbian - that it is in the name of Zdravko Tolimir, colonel. And this one has a ZT as the drafter, and who would that be as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time it would be Colonel Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And again we can see this has to do with prisoner exchanges. And the first line says: "Carry out all preparations for talks with the enemy side about a comprehensive exchange of POWs, captured civilians in the territory under the enemy's control, and bodies of dead Serbian soldiers." So what kind of document is this? Is that a directive in nature to these people it's -- or is it just for information or what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. This is directive in nature to the intelligence department of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now if we could go to the next page in English. And we see in the original somebody seems to have underlined the original, and that is reflected in the translation. And it says: "Prisoners from Vlasenica guarded by the MUP should not be shown for familiar reasons." Do you know what the -- and I don't want you to speculate, but do you know what the familiar reasons are that General Tolimir is referring to here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this particular order, no, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Does this -- so in 16 June 1994, does General Tolimir and his staff continue to be involved in prisoner exchange issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 3922 shall be assigned Exhibit P2486. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P2272 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another prisoner exchange issue document from the Main Staff sector for intel and security in the name of now assistant commander Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. And it begins after saying: "Prisoner exchange authorisation. "We authorise the representatives of POW exchange commissions from the Drina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps to establish contact on the front line with the prisoner exchange representatives of the 2nd Muslim Corps." What does this indicate to you the role of General Tolimir in dealing with prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is both an active and informed participant in this process. He is directing how these processes will take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I don't think I'll ask you to get into the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I would offer that into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I see there's a P in front of it, yes, thank you, as there is the next document which I would like us to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only wish to draw attention to the following. This is a draft translation and the sentence that was just read out in Serbian is "we are in agreement that ..." whereas in the English translation it says "we authorise that ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. We are looking forward to receiving the final, authorised translation. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given that possible explanation or possible alternative for -- meaning, what is your view -- who has the final say in prisoner exchange issues from your review of these documents and your knowledge of the situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately it's the commanders, the commander of the Main Staff. If one were to look back at the previous document, which is the 16 June 1994 document, one of the lines that's specifically used where addressing the issue to the commission of exchange is that the Main Staff is making it clear that it is not up to them to decide who -- it is not up to the exchange commission to decide who will be exchanged. That decision must be made by the corps commander on the basis of all relevant facts put before him by the security organs. So it's ultimately the commander's responsibilities. In this context General Tolimir presumably is speaking on behalf of and with the authority of the commander, General Mladic, when he relates these instructions to the subordinate formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, then if we go through this document -- I won't go over each of the directions in there, but let's go to page 3 in the English and it's the last -- should be the last page of the B/C/S where you can see the signature -- or the signature block. And we probably have to go to the next -- the previous page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 45, line 16, I notice in the transcript and I heard in the interpretation that the witness mentioned the corps commander. I would like to ask Mr. Peter McCloskey to clarify whether this was a slip of the tongue or whether this is actually the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, if we can go to that section - I think we can clear it up - in the document I was referring to.
